Theoretical Macroeconomics

A complete reading on dynamic macroeconomics: from growth models and dynamic programming through labour-market search, complete and incomplete markets, asset pricing and consumption theory, to real business cycles, monetary models and New Keynesian economics, ending with optimal monetary policy. Textbooks often split these into separate "growth", "cycles" and "money" courses that feel like different models. The view taken here is that modern macro has a single skeleton — preferences + technology + market structure + shocks — solved with one toolkit (Lagrangians and Bellman equations, Euler equations, log-linearisation). Each chapter first says what question is asked and why it is modelled this way, then gives equations and derivations, and finally computes the simplest closed-form example.

Prerequisites: calculus and linear algebra, basic probability (conditional expectation, Markov chains), and first-year microeconomics (consumer and firm optimisation, competitive equilibrium).

What this text will let you do

After reading you should be able to:

  1. Read a macro model as four blocks (preferences, technology, market structure, shocks) and write down its optimisation problem and Euler equation (Chapters 0–3).
  2. Compute a steady state and a transition path by hand for the Solow and neoclassical growth models, and solve the log-utility growth model in closed form (Chapters 1–2).
  3. Compute a reservation wage, a market-tightness equilibrium, a stochastic discount factor and a risk premium from a few numbers (Chapters 4–6).
  4. Explain consumption smoothing, precautionary saving and why incomplete markets change the interest rate (Chapters 7–8).
  5. Linearise a model, check the Blanchard–Kahn condition and read a policy function (Chapter 9).
  6. Use the New Keynesian model: compute the slope of the Phillips curve, check the Taylor principle, and compare discretion with commitment (Chapters 11–13).

How to read.

  • Every chapter opens with a box Intuition: the question the chapter answers, in plain words.
  • Each core idea is followed by a Worked example with small numbers. Do the arithmetic yourself; every step is shown. All numbers are for illustration, not calibrated to any country.
  • Paragraphs that start with Proof can be skipped on a first reading; each important proof is preceded by a one-sentence summary (In one sentence).
  • Sections marked Advanced go beyond what later chapters need; skip them freely.
  • The last three chapters collect common misconceptions, exercises with answers and a glossary.

Notation

  • c_t,k_t,n_t are consumption, capital, labour; y_t=f(k_t) or zF(K,N) output; \delta depreciation; \beta the discount factor; U(\cdot) utility.
  • \hat x_t=\ln(x_t/\bar x)\approx(x_t-\bar x)/\bar x is the log deviation; \bar x the steady-state value.
  • S_t is the state, S^t=(S_0,\dots,S_t) the history, \pi(S'\mid S) the transition probability, E_t[\cdot] the expectation given date-t information.
  • V(\cdot) is a value function, g(\cdot) a policy function; \mathbb 1\{\cdot\} an indicator.

0. The Big Picture: What Is Macroeconomics About?

0.1 One skeleton

Intuition. Picture a society of many "micro agents" (households, firms, government). Each makes optimal intertemporal choices: consume or save today? hire or not? raise the price or not? Each choice affects the others through prices (interest rates, wages, the price level) and aggregation (total capital, total output). Macroeconomics puts these optimal choices together, finds the equilibrium, and asks how it evolves over time, how it responds to shocks, and whether policy can improve it.

Every model is built from four blocks:

Block Example
Preferences households maximise E_0\sum\beta^tU(c_t,n_t)
Technology Y=zF(K,N); capital accumulation K'=(1-\delta)K+I
Market structure planner? competition? complete markets (Arrow securities)? incomplete markets (one asset)? sticky prices?
Shocks technology z, income y, cost-push e; usually Markov processes

0.2 Three big questions

  1. Long run: why are some countries rich and others poor? How do saving, technology and population determine long-run income? (growth theory, Chapter 1)
  2. Short run: why does the economy fluctuate? How do people smooth consumption? How do asset prices reflect risk? (consumption, asset pricing, RBC, Chapters 5–10)
  3. Policy: why does money matter? How should a central bank set interest rates? (monetary models, New Keynesian economics, optimal monetary policy, Chapters 11–13)

0.3 Toolbox

Tool Solves Chapter

Dynamic programming (Bellman) makes infinite-horizon problems recursive 2, 3
Contraction mapping, Blackwell conditions existence/uniqueness and computability of the Bellman solution 2
Markov chains describing random shocks 3
Log-linearisation + Blanchard–Kahn solving dynamic systems with no closed form 1, 9
Numerics: value-function iteration, shooting, simulation Huggett / Aiyagari / Krusell–Smith 8

Four small economies return again and again; all parameters are illustrative.

Example Numbers Where

A sense of scale. Real-world macro models are solved on a computer. The examples here are chosen so that every number can be checked by hand; the computer only repeats the same steps many times.

1. Growth Models

Intuition. Why is an American today richer than a hundred years ago, or than people in many countries? Growth theory answers: capital accumulation equips each worker with more machines, but diminishing marginal returns mean accumulation alone cannot sustain growth forever — in the end it is technology that does. We start with the simplest model, Solow (saving rate exogenous), then the neoclassical growth model where households choose saving optimally.

1.1 The Solow model

Assumptions:

  • capital accumulation: K_{t+1}=(1-\delta)K_t+I_t;
  • exogenous saving: I_t=sY_t;
  • technology: Y_t=F(K_t,A_tL_t), A_{t+1}=(1+g)A_t (labour-augmenting technical progress);
  • F satisfies the Inada conditions: F(0,0)=0, F_K,F_L>0, F_{KK},F_{LL}<0, constant returns, marginal products infinite at 0 and zero at infinity.

A steady state is where all endogenous variables stop changing. The golden rule is the saving rate maximising steady-state consumption.

Solution.

  1. Detrend: let k_t=K_t/(A_tL_t), y_t=Y_t/(A_tL_t)=f(k_t). Then
    (1+g)k_{t+1}=(1-\delta)k_t+sf(k_t).
  2. Steady state: k_{t+1}=k_t=k gives (g+\delta)k=sf(k). The left side is a line, the right side strictly increasing and strictly concave; Inada conditions guarantee exactly one positive intersection k^*.
  3. Golden rule: steady-state consumption c=(1-s)f(k(s))=f(k)-(g+\delta)k; the first-order condition
    f'(k^{\rm gold})=g+\delta
    fixes the golden-rule capital and hence the optimal saving rate.
  4. Conditional convergence: capital growth \dfrac{k_{t+1}-k_t}{k_t}\approx\dfrac{sf(k_t)}{k_t}-(g+\delta), and f(k)/k falls with k, so poorer countries (smaller k) grow faster.

Example (Cobb–Douglas, f=k^\alpha, g=0). k^*=\big(\dfrac s\delta\big)^{1/(1-\alpha)}; golden rule \alpha k^{\alpha-1}=\delta, i.e. s^{\rm gold}=\alpha (saving rate = capital share).

Worked example (Solow, in numbers). Take f(k)=k^{1/3}, g=0, \delta=0.1 and saving rate s=0.3. The steady state solves 0.1\,k=0.3\,k^{1/3}, so k^{*}=(0.3/0.1)^{1.5}=3^{1.5}\approx5.20, output y^*=k^{*1/3}=\sqrt3\approx1.73 and consumption c^*=(1-0.3)\cdot1.73\approx1.21. The golden-rule saving rate is s=\alpha=\tfrac13, with k^{\rm gold}=(\tfrac13/0.1)^{1.5}\approx6.09 and c=1.826-0.1\cdot6.09\approx1.217: only slightly above 1.21, because consumption is flat near its maximum.

Transition. Start from k_0=1 (a poor country): k_1=0.9\cdot1+0.3\cdot1=1.2 (growth 20%), k_2=0.9\cdot1.2+0.3\cdot1.2^{1/3}=1.399 (16.6%), k_3=1.594 (14.0%). Start from k_0=4 (a rich country): k_1=0.9\cdot4+0.3\cdot4^{1/3}=4.076 (growth only 1.9%). Conditional convergence: both approach the same k^*, but the poor country grows much faster along the way.

1.2 The neoclassical growth model (Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans)

Intuition. In Solow the saving rate is "pulled from the air". The neoclassical growth model lets a social planner (or representative household) trade off consuming today against more capital tomorrow. Save a bit more, eat a bit less now, and tomorrow there is more capital and output. At the optimum the utility lost by giving up a unit of consumption today equals the utility gained from the extra capital tomorrow — this is the Euler equation.

Problem:

\max\sum_{t=0}^\infty\beta^tU(C_t)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad K_{t+1}+C_t=F(K_t,A_tL_t)+(1-\delta)K_t.
U is strictly increasing and strictly concave with Inada conditions.

Solution (no growth or population growth to expose the logic).

  1. Lagrangian: \mathcal L=\sum\beta^t[U(c_t)+\lambda_t(f(k_t)+(1-\delta)k_t-k_{t+1}-c_t)]; first-order conditions
    U'(c_t)=\beta U'(c_{t+1})\big[f'(k_{t+1})+1-\delta\big]\quad(\text{Euler equation}),\qquad k_{t+1}+c_t=f(k_t)+(1-\delta)k_t.
  2. Transversality condition: \lim_{t\to\infty}\beta^tU'(c_t)k_{t+1}=0 (capital may not be hoarded forever unused).
  3. Steady state: f'(\bar k)=\dfrac1\beta-1+\delta (the modified golden rule: impatience makes capital smaller than the golden rule), \bar c=f(\bar k)-\delta\bar k.
  4. Phase diagram: the Euler equation says that when k_t<\bar k, f' is higher so c rises; feasibility says that when c_t<\bar c, k rises. The curves \Delta c=0 and \Delta k=0 split the plane into four regions and only one stable arm leads to the steady state.

Why is only the stable arm optimal? Given k_0 the household could choose different c_0. If c_0 is too high capital is eventually exhausted, violating feasibility; if too low capital accumulates forever, violating transversality ("saving that is never eaten"). So the unique optimal path is the stable arm: saddle-path stability.

Log-linearisation and solving the linear system. There is rarely a closed form, so linearise around the steady state with \hat x_t=\ln(x_t/\bar x). Lemma: if y=f(x) then \hat y=\dfrac{\bar xf'(\bar x)}{f(\bar x)}\hat x (an elasticity). The Euler equation and resource constraint become

\begin{pmatrix}\hat c_{t+1}\\\hat k_{t+1}\end{pmatrix}=M\begin{pmatrix}\hat c_t\\\hat k_t\end{pmatrix}.

  1. Find the eigenvalues of M: if (\lambda_1-1)(\lambda_2-1)<0 one is <1 and one >1 (a saddle).
  2. Decompose M=VDV^{-1}. Let z_t=V_{21}\hat c_t+V_{22}\hat k_t (associated with the unstable eigenvalue \lambda_2>1); then z_{t+1}=\lambda_2z_t. If z_t\ne0 the system explodes (violating feasibility or transversality), so z_t=0, giving the policy function
    \hat c_t=-V_{21}^{-1}V_{22}\,\hat k_t,\qquad\hat k_{t+1}=(M_{22}-M_{21}V_{21}^{-1}V_{22})\hat k_t.

This "eliminate the unstable direction" step is the seed of the Blanchard–Kahn method of Chapter 9.

Worked example (the modified golden rule). Now let households choose saving: \beta=0.96, \delta=0.1, f=k^{1/3}. The steady state needs f'(\bar k)=1/\beta-1+\delta=0.0417+0.1=0.1417, i.e. \tfrac13\bar k^{-2/3}=0.1417, so \bar k=3.61 and \bar c=\bar k^{1/3}-0.1\bar k=1.534-0.361=1.173. Impatience (\beta<1) makes the optimal capital (3.61) smaller than the golden-rule capital (6.09): the planner does not sacrifice present consumption for the last bit of steady-state consumption.

2. Deterministic Dynamic Programming

Intuition. An infinite-horizon problem looks like choosing infinitely many variables \{x_t\}. The insight of dynamic programming: whatever the past, optimal choices from today on depend only on today's state. So split the problem into "today + value of tomorrow", a recursive problem V(x)=\max_y\{F(x,y)+\beta V(y)\}. The key mathematical questions: does this functional equation have a solution? Is it unique? How do we compute it? The answer is — the contraction mapping.

2.1 Mathematical preliminaries

Advanced section: it explains why the Bellman equation has a unique solution. The conclusion (a solution exists, is unique, and iteration finds it) is all that later chapters use.

Contraction: T:X\to X is a contraction if some \beta\in[0,1) has d(Tx,Ty)\le\beta d(x,y).

Contraction mapping theorem: on a complete metric space a contraction has a unique fixed point, and iterating T from any starting point converges to it.

Worked example (a contraction in one dimension). T(x)=0.5x+1 satisfies |T(x)-T(y)|=0.5|x-y|, so \beta=0.5. Its fixed point solves x=0.5x+1, i.e. x=2. Starting from x_0=0 the iterates are 1,\ 1.5,\ 1.75,\ 1.875,\ 1.9375,\dots: the distance to 2 halves each step. The Bellman operator behaves in the same way, with functions instead of numbers.

Blackwell's sufficient conditions: let T act on bounded functions B(X) with the sup norm. If

  1. monotonicity: f\le g\Rightarrow Tf\le Tg;
  2. discounting: there is \beta<1 with T(f+a)\le Tf+\beta a (a\ge0); then T is a contraction.

Intuition. The Bellman operator satisfies both: a larger value function makes today's choices better (monotonicity), and every future value is multiplied by \beta<1 (discounting). So instead of checking a complicated distance condition we only check "monotone + discounting".

Theorem of the maximum: if F is continuous and the constraint correspondence \Gamma is compact-valued and continuous, the maximised value function is continuous and the policy correspondence is non-empty and upper hemicontinuous.

In one sentence. If an operator is monotone and shrinks every constant shift by \beta<1, then applying it twice to two functions at most \beta times as far apart each time, so repeated application converges to one fixed point.

2.2 The Bellman equation and its properties

V(x)=\sup_{y\in\Gamma(x)}\{F(x,y)+\beta V(y)\}.
Assumptions Conclusion
1–2: \Gamma non-empty, compact, continuous; F bounded and continuous V exists, unique, continuous, bounded
3–4: F strictly increasing in x; \Gamma monotone V strictly increasing
5–6: F strictly concave; \Gamma convex V strictly concave; policy is a single-valued function
7: F differentiable V differentiable, V'(x)=F_x(x,g(x)) (envelope theorem)

Principle of optimality: under assumptions 1–2 a solution of the sequential problem \sup\sum\beta^tF(x_t,x_{t+1}) solves the recursive problem; conversely a bounded solution of the recursive problem with \lim\beta^nV(x_n)=0 solves the sequential problem.

2.3 Three solution methods

  1. Euler-equation method: the first-order condition F_y(x,y)+\beta V'(y)=0 plus the envelope condition V'(x)=F_x(x,y) give the Euler equation
    F_y(x,g(x))+\beta F_x(g(x),g(g(x)))=0.
  2. Guess and verify: guess a functional form for V (or the policy), plug it into the Bellman equation and solve for parameters by undetermined coefficients.
  3. Value-function iteration: start from any v_0, set v_{i+1}=Tv_i until d(v_{i+1},v_i)<\epsilon.

2.4 Examples

Example 1: tree cutting. A tree grows k_{t+1}=k_t^\alpha (\alpha<1); each period choose to cut or wait: V(k)=\max\{k,\ \beta V(k^\alpha)\}. Iterating: V_0=0 ⟹ always cut; V_1=k ⟹ cut if k>\bar k (\bar k=\beta\bar k^\alpha), otherwise wait one period; further iterations change nothing. Conclusion: if you will cut, cut tomorrow — waiting one more period only slows growth (\beta^2k^{\alpha^2}<\beta k^\alpha). V(k)=\bar k for k<\bar k and k otherwise.

Example 2: log utility, Cobb–Douglas growth (Brock–Mirman, closed form).

V(k)=\max_{k'}\ \ln(k^\alpha-k')+\beta V(k').

  • Contraction check: monotonicity — if f\ge h, T(h)\le T(f) (use h's optimal choice in f); discounting — T(f+a)=Tf+\beta a. By Blackwell it is a contraction.
  • Euler equation: \dfrac1{k^\alpha-k'}=\beta\dfrac{\alpha k'^{\alpha-1}}{k'^\alpha-k''}.
  • Guess V(k)=A\ln k+B: the first-order condition \dfrac1{k^\alpha-k'}=\dfrac{\beta A}{k'} gives k'=\dfrac{\beta A}{1+\beta A}k^\alpha. Matching coefficients on \ln k gives A=\alpha(1+\beta A), i.e.
    A=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha\beta},\qquad k'=\alpha\beta\,k^\alpha.
    Result: the household saves the fixed fraction \alpha\beta of output each period (Solow's fixed saving rate is optimal in this special case).

Example 3: an extra asset. V(k,a)=\max\ln(k^\alpha+ra-k'-a')+\beta V(k',a'). The point: Blackwell's conditions still verify the contraction, so a unique solution exists.

Worked example (value-function iteration by hand). In Example 2 start from V_0=0. Then V_1(k)=\max\ln(k^\alpha-k')+0 is attained at k'=0 and equals \alpha\ln k (eat everything in the last period). Write V_n=A_n\ln k+B_n. Maximising \ln(k^\alpha-k')+\beta A_n\ln k' gives A_{n+1}=\alpha(1+\beta A_n). With \alpha=\tfrac13, \beta=0.96:

A_1=0.333,\quad A_2=0.440,\quad A_3=0.474,\quad A_4=0.485,\quad A_5=0.489,\ \dots\ \to\ A=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha\beta}=0.490.
So the iteration converges to the closed-form answer.

Worked example (the closed-form growth path). The saving rate is \alpha\beta=0.32. Start from k_0=1: output 1, saving k_1=0.32, consumption 0.68. Next k_2=0.32\cdot0.32^{1/3}=0.219 (output 0.684, consumption 0.465), then k_3=0.193. Capital converges to \bar k=(\alpha\beta)^{1/(1-\alpha)}=0.32^{1.5}=0.181. The economy shrinks towards a small steady state because \beta=0.96 discounts the future and capital depreciates fully in this special case.

3. Stochastic Dynamic Programming

Intuition. The future is uncertain: technology is sometimes good, sometimes bad. Stochastic dynamic programming is nearly identical to the deterministic version once "tomorrow's value" is replaced by a conditional expectation. The difference: a random system has no steady-state point but converges to a stationary distribution.

3.1 Markov processes

  • A Markov chain \{S_t\} takes finitely many values with P(S_{t+1}\mid S^t)=P(S_{t+1}\mid S_t). It is described by (S,P,\psi_0): the state values, the transition matrix P_{ij}=P(S_{t+1}=s_j|S_t=s_i) (rows sum to 1), and the initial distribution \psi_0.
  • Unconditional distribution: \psi_t=(P')^t\psi_0.
  • Stationary distribution: \psi^*=P'\psi^*, i.e. (I-P')\psi^*=0 and \sum\psi_i^*=1.
  • Conditional expectation: E_t[S_{t+1}]=\sum_jP_{ij}s_j.

Example (two states). P=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.1\\0.2&0.8\end{pmatrix}: the stationary distribution satisfies \psi_1^*=0.9\psi_1^*+0.2\psi_2^*, so \psi^*=(2/3,1/3).

Worked example (how a Markov chain forgets its start). With P=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.1\\0.2&0.8\end{pmatrix} start in state 1: \psi_0=(1,0). Then \psi_1=(0.9,0.1), \psi_2=(0.83,0.17), \psi_3=(0.781,0.219), \psi_4=(0.747,0.253), approaching (2/3,1/3). State 1 lasts on average 1/0.1=10 periods, state 2 lasts 1/0.2=5 periods: the stationary shares 2/3 and 1/3 are just the ratio of the two durations 10:5.

3.2 The stochastic Bellman equation

V(x,z)=\sup_{y\in\Gamma(x,z)}\Big\{F(x,y,z)+\beta E[V(y,z')\mid z]\Big\}.

All the properties of the Bellman equation survive. The policy y=g(x,z) solves a stochastic difference equation; there is no steady-state point, instead the endogenous variables have a stationary distribution computable from the policy function and the shock's transition probabilities.

3.3 The stochastic growth model

Setup: a planner; total factor productivity z_t follows a Markov chain; k_{t+1}+c_t=zf(k_t)+(1-\delta)k_t.

Sequential problem (summing over all histories z^t): \max\sum_t\sum_{z^t}\beta^tU(c_t(z^t))\pi(z^t). The first-order conditions combine into the stochastic Euler equation

U'(c_t)=\beta E_t\Big[U'(c_{t+1})\big(z_{t+1}f'(k_{t+1})+1-\delta\big)\Big].

Recursive problem: V(k,z)=\max\{U(c)+\beta\sum_{z'}V(k',z')\pi(z'|z)\}; the envelope condition V_k(k,z)=U'(c)[zf'(k)+1-\delta] gives the same Euler equation. Solve the stochastic difference system for c(k,z) and k'(k,z).

Worked example (stochastic growth with a closed form). Log utility and full depreciation give the saving rule k'=\alpha\beta\,z\,k^\alpha: the saving rate \alpha\beta=0.32 does not depend on the shock. Start from k=0.2 (k^{1/3}=0.585): in a good state z=1.1 next capital is 0.32\cdot1.1\cdot0.585=0.206, in a bad state z=0.9 it is 0.168. Capital therefore moves up and down with productivity and has a distribution rather than a single steady-state value.

4. Labour Markets and Search

Intuition. In a Walrasian market there is no unemployment if wages are low enough. But reality has "frictions": finding a job takes time and good jobs do not show up instantly. Search models treat unemployment as an investment: the unemployed turn down low wages and wait for better offers, because the cost of waiting (one period's income) is smaller than the expected gain. We start with the simplest McCall model and move to the labour-market general equilibrium of Diamond–Mortensen–Pissarides.

4.1 The McCall model

Setup: a risk-neutral worker receives a wage offer w\sim F, w\in[0,B], each period; accepting means working forever; rejecting yields unemployment income b and a new draw next period.

V(w)=\max\{\underbrace{w+\beta V(w)}_{\text{accept}},\ \underbrace{b+\beta E[V(w')]}_{\text{reject}}\}.

Reservation wage. Let \bar V=b+\beta E[V(w')] (a constant independent of the current w). The value of accepting \frac{w}{1-\beta} rises with w, so there is a reservation wage \bar w: accept iff w\ge\bar w, with \bar w/(1-\beta)=\bar V.

Finding \bar w.

\bar V=b+\beta\int_0^{\bar w}\bar V\,dF+\beta\int_{\bar w}^BV(w')dF=b+\beta\bar V+\beta\int_{\bar w}^B\frac{w'-\bar w}{1-\beta}dF(w').
Multiplying by (1-\beta),
\bar w=b+\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\int_{\bar w}^B(w'-\bar w)\,dF(w').

Meaning: reservation wage = unemployment income + the expected gain from continued search (counting only offers better than \bar w).

Let R(x)=\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\int_x^B(w'-x)dF(w'). By the Newton–Leibniz formula: R(0)=\frac\beta{1-\beta}E[w], R(B)=0, R'(x)=-\frac\beta{1-\beta}(1-F(x))<0, R''(x)=\frac\beta{1-\beta}f(x)>0. So R is strictly decreasing and strictly convex while x-b is an increasing line: they cross exactly once.

Comparative statics:

  1. b\uparrow ⟹ the line x-b moves down ⟹ \bar w\uparrow (more generous benefits, choosier);
  2. \beta\uparrow ⟹ R(x) moves up ⟹ \bar w\uparrow (more patient, choosier);
  3. G\le F (G first-order dominates F) ⟹ R moves up ⟹ \bar w\uparrow (better opportunities, higher asking wage);
  4. a more dispersed distribution (mean-preserving spread) ⟹ \bar w\uparrow (option value: ignore the bad, pick the good).

The last two follow by integrating by parts: \bar w-b=\beta(B-b)-\beta\int_{\bar w}^BF(w')dw' and \bar w-b=\beta(E[w']-b)+\beta\int_0^{\bar w}F(w')dw'.

Worked example (a reservation wage). Wage offers are uniform on [0,2], b=0.5, \beta=0.95. For the uniform distribution \int_{\bar w}^2(w-\bar w)\,\tfrac12dw=\tfrac{(2-\bar w)^2}4, so

\bar w=0.5+\frac{0.95}{0.05}\cdot\frac{(2-\bar w)^2}{4}=0.5+4.75\,(2-\bar w)^2.
Put u=2-\bar w: 4.75u^2+u-1.5=0, u=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{1+28.5}}{9.5}=0.4665, so \bar w\approx1.53. The worker accepts only offers in [1.53,2]: probability 0.4665/2=0.233 per period, so the expected unemployment spell is 1/0.233\approx4.3 periods. A larger benefit b=1 raises the reservation wage to 1.63 (acceptance falls to 18%): more generous benefits make workers choosier.

Check of the economic logic. Rejecting the lowest offers costs one period's lost wage but allows one to wait for a better one; the reservation wage is exactly where these two forces balance.

4.2 Variants of McCall

Advanced section.

  • Risk of being fired (probability \delta per period; the fired stay unemployed that period):
    V(w)=\max\{w+\beta(\delta U+(1-\delta)V(w)),\ U\},\quad\bar w=b+\frac{\beta}{1-\beta(1-\delta)}\int_{\bar w}^B(w-\bar w)dF(w).
    Firing risk discounts the value of accepting, so \bar w falls (easier to accept).
  • Wage growth (employed wages rise by g per period): value of accepting w/(1-\beta(1+g)), reservation wage \dfrac{1-\beta}{1-\beta(1+g)}\bar w=b+\dfrac\beta{1-\beta(1+g)}\int_{\bar w}^B(w'-\bar w)dF.
  • Changing environment (good and bad states; the worker may quit and search again): there are now two reservation wages \bar w(G),\bar w(B); the wage distribution is worse in the bad state, so people are reluctant to leave their jobs.

4.3 The Diamond–Mortensen–Pissarides (DMP) model

Intuition. In McCall the probability of meeting a job is exogenous. In reality firms create jobs: firms post vacancies (at a cost), unemployed workers and vacancies meet through a matching function, and the pair bargain over the wage. In equilibrium firms enter until the expected profit from posting a vacancy is zero (free entry).

Setup:

  • unemployment rate u, vacancy rate v; matching function M(u,v) increasing, concave, constant returns;
  • market tightness \theta=v/u; job-finding rate f(\theta)=M(u,v)/u=M(1,\theta); vacancy-filling rate q(\theta)=M(u,v)/v=f(\theta)/\theta;
  • separation probability \delta per period; a matched firm produces z; posting a vacancy costs kz; free entry; the wage is set by Nash bargaining with workers' bargaining power \phi.

Law of motion and Beveridge curve: u_{t+1}=\delta(1-u_t)+(1-f(\theta_t))u_t; in steady state u=\dfrac{\delta}{\delta+f(\theta)}, giving the Beveridge curve (negative relation between u and v).

Bellman equations (steady state):

\begin{aligned}W&=w+\beta(\delta U+(1-\delta)W),&U&=b+\beta(f(\theta)W+(1-f(\theta))U),\\J&=z-w+\beta(\delta V+(1-\delta)J),&V&=-kz+\beta(q(\theta)J+(1-q(\theta))V),\end{aligned}
where W,U are the values of employment and unemployment and J,V the firm's values with a worker and with a vacancy.

Solution.

  1. Free entry V=0: kz=\beta q(\theta)J. Substituting J=\dfrac{z-w}{1-\beta(1-\delta)} gives the tightness curve (job-creation condition)
    w=z-\big(1-\beta(1-\delta)\big)\frac{kz}{\beta q(\theta)}.
    (The tighter the market, the harder and costlier it is to fill a vacancy, so the less wage the firm can afford.)
  2. Nash bargaining \max(W-U)^\phi(J-V)^{1-\phi} gives \phi(J-V)=(1-\phi)(W-U). Substituting W,J: w=\phi z+(1-\phi)(1-\beta)U. Using the unemployed's Bellman equation (1-\beta)U=b+\beta f(\theta)(W-U) and f/q=\theta yields the wage curve
    w=(1-\phi)b+\phi(1+k\theta)z.
    (The worker gets a (1-\phi) share of the benefit, plus a share of output and of the "recruiting cost saved".)
  3. Solve the two curves for (w,\theta); the Beveridge curve then gives u and v.

Worked example (the DMP equilibrium in numbers). Illustrative parameters: z=1, b=0.4, \phi=0.5, \beta=0.95, separation \delta=0.1, vacancy cost k=0.3, matching M=0.5\sqrt{uv} so f(\theta)=0.5\sqrt\theta and q(\theta)=0.5/\sqrt\theta. The job-creation curve is w=1-(1-0.95\cdot0.9)\cdot0.3/(0.95\,q) and the wage curve is w=0.2+0.5(1+0.3\theta). Equating them gives tightness \theta\approx1.30 and wage w\approx0.895. Then f=0.571 (a searcher finds a job with probability 57% a period), q=0.438 (a vacancy is filled with probability 44%), unemployment u=\delta/(\delta+f)=0.149 and vacancies v=\theta u=0.194. A rise in unemployment benefits b shifts up the wage curve, lowers tightness and raises unemployment.

5. Complete Markets and the Welfare Theorems

Intuition. If there is an "insurance contract" (a contingent claim) for every possible future state, households can fully hedge idiosyncratic risk, and relative consumption shares no longer move with individual luck: whatever your own luck, your consumption is a fixed share of total consumption. This is a very strong result, and it lets us use a representative household to study aggregates.

5.1 Arrow–Debreu equilibrium

Setup:

  • I consumers in a stochastic endowment economy; e_t^i(S^t) is i's endowment after history S^t; common utility U; Markov states \pi(S'|S);
  • complete markets: a contingent claim (price p_t^0(S^t)) for consumption after every history; all trade takes place once at date 0, never again.

Consumer problem:

\max\sum_t\sum_{S^t}\beta^tU(C_t^i(S^t))\pi(S^t)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_t\sum_{S^t}p_t^0(S^t)C_t^i(S^t)\le\sum_t\sum_{S^t}p_t^0(S^t)e_t^i(S^t).
Equilibrium: prices \{p_t^0\} and allocations \{C_t^i\} such that ①each agent optimises given prices; ②markets clear after every history, \sum_iC_t^i(S^t)=\sum_ie_t^i(S^t).

Solution.

  1. First-order condition \beta^tU'(C_t^i(S^t))\pi(S^t)=\mu^ip_t^0(S^t). Dividing for two agents gives \dfrac{U'(C^i_t)}{U'(C^j_t)}=\dfrac{\mu^i}{\mu^j}, independent of time and state. So consumption shares are constant:
    C_t^i(S^t)=\tilde\mu^iY_t(S^t),\qquad\sum_i\tilde\mu^i=1,
    where Y_t=\sum_ie^i_t is the aggregate endowment. This is risk sharing.
  2. Prices: p_t^0(S^t)=\beta^t\dfrac{U'(Y_t(S^t))}{U'(Y_0)}\pi(S^t|S_0)\,p_0^0. (In states with low aggregate output marginal utility, and hence state prices, are high.)
  3. Shares: \tilde\mu^i=\dfrac{\sum p^0_te^i_t}{\sum p_t^0Y_t}, the present value of i's endowment as a fraction of the aggregate.

Worked example (risk sharing in two states). One period, two equally likely states, log utility. Aggregate endowment is 3 in the good state H and 1 in the bad state L. Agent 1 has endowments (2,1), agent 2 has (1,0). State prices are proportional to \pi_s/Y_s: p_H=\tfrac12/3=\tfrac16, p_L=\tfrac12/1=\tfrac12 (a dollar is worth more in the bad state). Present values: agent 1: 2\cdot\tfrac16+1\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac56; agent 2: 1\cdot\tfrac16=\tfrac16; total 1. So the shares are \tilde\mu^1=\tfrac56, \tilde\mu^2=\tfrac16 and consumption is c^1=(2.5,\ 0.833), c^2=(0.5,\ 0.167): each consumes a fixed share of the aggregate whatever the state. Agent 2 has no endowment in state L yet consumes 0.167: the insurance contract pays for it. Check agent 1's budget: she receives 0.5 in H (worth 0.5/6=0.083) and pays 0.167 in L (worth 0.167\cdot0.5=0.083).

5.2 Sequential markets (Arrow securities)

Setup: the same economy, but each period agents trade Arrow securities: pay \tilde q_t(S^t,S') for a claim paying 1 next period only in state S'.

C_t^i(S^t)+\sum_{S'}\tilde q_t(S^t,S')a^i_{t+1}(S^t,S')\le e^i_t(S^t)+a_t^i(S^{t-1},S_t),\qquad a^i_{t+1}\ge-\bar A\ (\text{No-Ponzi}).
The first-order conditions give the Euler equation for security prices
\tilde q_t(S^t,S')=\beta\frac{U'(Y_{t+1}(S^t,S'))}{U'(Y_t(S^t))}\pi(S'|S^t)=\frac{p^0_{t+1}(S^t,S')}{p^0_t(S^t)}.

Theorem (equivalence). The sequential-markets equilibrium has the same allocation as the Arrow–Debreu equilibrium.

In one sentence. Adding up the period budgets with the no-Ponzi condition gives exactly one lifetime budget, the same as in the Arrow–Debreu economy, so the two economies have the same solution.

Proof (add up discounted budget constraints). Let P^0_t(S^t)=\prod_{j<t}\tilde q_j. Summing all discounted sequential budgets, the No-Ponzi condition kills the terminal term and gives the lifetime budget \sum P^0_tC_t^i\le\sum P^0_te^i_t, identical to Arrow–Debreu's; the latter has a unique solution, so the two coincide. \square

5.3 The social planner and welfare theorems

Planner's problem: \max\sum_t\sum_{S^t}\sum_i\beta^t\lambda^iU(C_t^i)\pi(S^t) s.t. resources, with exogenous \lambda^i. The first-order condition \beta^t\lambda^iU'(C^i_t)\pi(S^t)=\phi_t(S^t) again gives constant consumption shares C^i_t=\tilde\lambda^iY_t.

First Welfare Theorem. An Arrow–Debreu equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient (and so is the sequential-markets allocation).

In one sentence. A better allocation would have to cost more than the whole economy is worth at the equilibrium prices, which is impossible.

Proof. A Pareto-dominating allocation would cost at least as much for everyone and strictly more for someone (else that person would have chosen it); adding up and using resources gives \sum p^0e>\sum p^0e, a contradiction. \square

Duality with the planner (a version of the Second Welfare Theorem). Choosing weights \lambda^i so that each person's net transfer T_i=0, the planner's solution is the competitive equilibrium.

Significance: under complete markets we can solve the competitive equilibrium by solving the planner's problem — a huge simplification.

6. Asset Pricing

Intuition. What is an asset worth? The present value of its future payoffs, discounted with a "stochastic discount factor". The SDF is "today's value of one unit of future consumption": in bad times (high marginal utility) a dollar is worth more, so assets that pay off in bad times are more valuable — they are insurance. Risk premia come from the covariance of returns with the SDF.

6.1 The Lucas tree

Setup: a representative household; a "tree" yields random dividends d_t each period; the household trades shares A_t (price P_t) and a one-period bond B_t (price Q_t).

\max E_0\sum\beta^tU(C_t)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad C_t+P_tA_t+Q_tB_t=(P_t+d_t)A_{t-1}+B_{t-1}.
Equilibrium: C_t=d_t, A_t=1, B_t=0.

First-order conditions and pricing equations:

Q_t=\beta E_t\Big[\frac{U'(d_{t+1})}{U'(d_t)}\Big],\qquad P_t=\beta E_t\Big[\frac{U'(d_{t+1})}{U'(d_t)}\big(P_{t+1}+d_{t+1}\big)\Big].
Stochastic discount factor: M_{t,t+1}=\beta\dfrac{U'(C_{t+1})}{U'(C_t)}; the pricing kernel is M_{t,t+1}\pi(S_{t+1}|S_t). Iterating forward,
P_t=\sum_{\tau>t}E_t\Big[\beta^{\tau-t}\frac{U'(d_\tau)}{U'(d_t)}d_\tau\Big]+\underbrace{\lim_T E_t[\cdots]}_{=0\ \text{(no bubbles)}}.

Worked example (pricing a tree). Log utility, \beta=0.96, dividends d_t follow any process. Then U'(d_{t+1})/U'(d_t)=d_t/d_{t+1} and the pricing equation is solved by P_t=\kappa d_t: \kappa d_t=\beta E_t[\tfrac{d_t}{d_{t+1}}(\kappa+1)d_{t+1}]=\beta(\kappa+1)d_t, so \kappa=\beta/(1-\beta)=24. The price–dividend ratio is 24 whatever the risk. If next dividend is 0.9 or 1.1 (equally likely) when d_t=1: the bond price is Q=0.96\cdot E[1/d']=0.96\cdot1.0101=0.9697, so R^f=1.0313. The stock return is R'=(P'+d')/P=(25/24)\,d', with mean 1.0417. The premium is only 1.0417-1.0313\approx1\% because dividends are almost uncorrelated with marginal utility in this tiny-risk example.

6.2 The term structure of interest rates

Add a two-period bond. One- and two-period bond prices are

Q_{1t}=\beta E_t\Big[\frac{U'(d_{t+1})}{U'(d_t)}\Big],\qquad Q_{2t}=\beta^2E_t\Big[\frac{U'(d_{t+2})}{U'(d_t)}\Big].

  • Holding-period return R_{t,t+j}=\dfrac{P_{t+j}+d_{t+j}}{P_t}; yield to maturity YTM_j=R_{t,t+j}^{1/j}.
  • Expectations hypothesis: Q_{2t}=Q_{1t}E_t[Q_{1,t+1}]. It generally fails (the two differ by a risk-related covariance term).
  • Long rates usually exceed short rates (a positive term premium); an inverted yield curve often predicts recession — households expect low future consumption and high marginal utility, and are willing to pay a lot for future purchasing power.

6.3 The consumption CAPM

Risk-neutral probabilities: \pi^r(S'|S)=\pi(S'|S)M(S')\big/\sum_{S'}M(S'). Then

P_t=E_t[M_{t+1}]\cdot E^r_t\big[P_{t+1}+d_{t+1}\big]\quad(\text{risk-neutral expectation discounted at the risk-free rate}).
Risk-free rate: \bar R_{t+1}=1/E_t[M_{t,t+1}].

Theorem (excess return). The pricing equation E_t[M_{t,t+1}R_{t+1}]=1 expands to \operatorname{cov}(M,R)+E[M]E[R]=1, so

E_t[R_{t+1}]-\bar R_{t+1}=-\bar R_{t+1}\operatorname{cov}_t(M_{t,t+1},R_{t+1}).

Intuition. An asset that pays well when consumption is low (high M) is "insurance", in high demand, with a high price and thus a low average return; conversely, assets that lose money in recessions (negatively correlated with M) must offer a positive risk premium to be held.

Bound on Sharpe ratios (Hansen–Jagannathan):

\Big|\frac{E[R_{t+1}-\bar R_{t+1}]}{\sigma(R)}\Big|\le\frac{\sigma(M)}{E[M]}.

In one sentence. The risk premium is the correlation between the SDF and the return times the SDF's volatility, and a correlation cannot exceed one in absolute value.

Proof: from the above, \dfrac{E[R]-\bar R}{\sigma_R}=-\dfrac{\sigma(M)}{E[M]}\operatorname{corr}(M,R) and |\operatorname{corr}|\le1. \square

6.4 The equity premium puzzle

Setup: \dfrac{C_{t+1}}{C_t}=\bar C_\Delta\exp(\epsilon_{c,t+1}-\sigma_c^2/2), 1+r_{t+1}=(1+\bar r)\exp(\epsilon_{r,t+1}-\sigma_r^2/2), jointly normal; CRRA utility U=c^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma).

From 1=\beta E[(1+r_{t+1})(C_{t+1}/C_t)^{-\gamma}], taking logs and evaluating the lognormal expectation,

\ln(1+\bar r)=-\ln\beta+\gamma\ln\bar C_\Delta-\tfrac12\gamma(1+\gamma)\sigma_c^2+\gamma\operatorname{cov}(\epsilon_r,\epsilon_c).
Subtracting the same expression for the risk-free asset (zero covariance):
\boxed{\ \ln(1+\bar r)-\ln(1+\bar r^f)=\gamma\,\operatorname{cov}(\epsilon_c,\epsilon_r)\ }.
The puzzle: in US data the equity premium is about 6% while the covariance of stock returns with consumption growth is only about 0.002. Matching the premium requires \gamma\approx 0.06/0.002\approx30, an order of magnitude above reasonable risk aversion (1–5). This is the Mehra–Prescott equity premium puzzle, the starting point of much asset-pricing research (habit formation, long-run risk, …).

Worked example (the size of the puzzle). With \gamma=1 (log utility) the formula gives a premium of 1\times0.002=0.2\% a year; the data show about 6%. Solving \gamma\cdot0.002=0.06 gives \gamma=30. Such a household would, for example, refuse a coin-flip gamble that doubles or cuts by 20% its wealth, since with \gamma=30 its certainty equivalent (0.82 of current wealth) is below what she holds now. This is why \gamma=30 is regarded as implausibly large.

6.5 Back to Arrow–Debreu asset pricing

Advanced section.

Add a tradable asset (a "tree") to the Arrow–Debreu economy. Equilibrium prices again satisfy P_t=\sum_{S'}\dfrac{p^0_{t+1}}{p^0_t}(P_{t+1}+d_{t+1}): an asset's price = present value of its dividends discounted at Arrow–Debreu state prices. Sequential markets give the same pricing equation with \tilde q_t the ratio of state prices; no-arbitrage rules out the bubble term.

7. Consumption Theory

Intuition. Keynes held that consumption depends on current income; Friedman and Modigliani objected: rational people smooth consumption — a one-off income change moves consumption only a little because they spread it over the rest of life; only permanent income changes move consumption much. This is the permanent-income hypothesis. The key question: how does a rational person save? Answer: to smooth, not to hoard.

7.1 The consumer problem and the Euler equation

Partial equilibrium: no production, one asset a_t with gross return R_t, exogenous random income y_t.

\max E_t\sum_{j}\beta^jU(c_{t+j})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad c_t+a_t=R_ta_{t-1}+y_t,\quad\lim_sE_t[a_{t+s}/R^s]=0\ (\text{weak No-Ponzi}).
Euler equation: U'(c_t)=\beta E_t[R_{t+1}U'(c_{t+1})].

7.2 The consumption martingale

Assume R=1/\beta (the interest rate exactly offsets impatience). Then U'(c_t)=E_t[U'(c_{t+1})]: marginal utility is a martingale. With quadratic utility U(c)=-\frac12(c-\gamma)^2, marginal utility is linear, so

c_t=E_t[c_{t+1}]\quad(\text{consumption is a martingale})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Delta c_{t+1}=\epsilon_{t+1},\ E_t\epsilon_{t+1}=0.
Implication: changes in consumption are unpredictable — no past variable (including past income changes) should predict them. A testable hypothesis: regress \Delta c_{t+1}=\beta\,E_t[\Delta y_{t+1}]+\epsilon_{t+1} and test \beta=0. (Data often find \beta>0: excess sensitivity, often attributed to liquidity constraints.)

7.3 The closed-form permanent-income solution

Discounting and summing the budget constraints with the weak No-Ponzi condition gives the lifetime budget constraint

(1+r)a_{t-1}=-E_t\sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{y_{t+j}-c_{t+j}}{(1+r)^j}.
By the martingale property c_t=E_t[c_{t+j}] for all j, so consumption is the constant c_t and
\boxed{\ c_t=r\,a_{t-1}+\frac r{1+r}\,E_t\sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{y_{t+j}}{(1+r)^j}\ }.

Reading: consumption = the "annuity value" of assets + the "annuity" of the present value of expected future income. People spread lifetime resources evenly over all periods.

Corollaries.

  • Saving s_t=a_t-a_{t-1}=y_t-\dfrac r{1+r}E_t\sum\dfrac{y_{t+j}}{(1+r)^j}=-E_t\sum_{j\ge1}\dfrac{\Delta y_{t+j}}{(1+r)^j}: saving = present value of expected future income declines (saving for a "rainy day").
  • Change in consumption \epsilon_{t+1}=\dfrac r{1+r}\sum_j\dfrac{(E_{t+1}-E_t)y_{t+j+1}}{(1+r)^j}: consumption reacts only to revisions of income expectations.
  • Ricardian equivalence (timing of lump-sum taxes is irrelevant) and certainty equivalence (only conditional means matter, not variances; hence no precautionary saving).

Example (AR(1) income): y_t=\rho y_{t-1}+e_t.

\rho=0 (purely transitory) \rho\in(0,1) \rho=1 (permanent)
c_t ra_{t-1}+\frac r{1+r}y_t ra_{t-1}+\frac r{1+r-\rho}y_t ra_{t-1}+y_t
s_t \frac1{1+r}y_t \frac{1-\rho}{1+r-\rho}y_t 0
\epsilon_{t+1} \frac r{1+r}y_t \frac r{1+r-\rho}y_t y_t

Intuition: a transitory income shock (\rho=0) is almost entirely saved (consumption rises by only \frac r{1+r}, about 5%); a permanent shock (\rho=1) is consumed entirely, with no saving.

Worked example (how much of a windfall is spent?). r=5\%, current assets zero. A one-off income rise of 1 (\rho=0): consumption rises by \dfrac r{1+r}=0.0476 and 0.952 is saved. If the rise is persistent with \rho=0.5: consumption rises by \dfrac r{1+r-\rho}=\dfrac{0.05}{0.55}=0.091. If it is permanent (\rho=1): consumption rises by 1, nothing is saved. What matters is how long the income change lasts. A 5% interest rate means one dollar today is an annuity of only about 5 cents a period, which is why a one-time windfall hardly changes consumption.

7.4 Precautionary saving

Failure of certainty equivalence: when the third derivative of utility is positive (U'''>0, called prudence) uncertainty makes people save more.

Two-period model: \max U(c_0)+\beta E[U(c_1)], c_0+a_1=y_0, c_1=Ra_1+y_1, E[y_1]=0, \operatorname{Var}(y_1)=\sigma^2, R\beta=1. Euler equation U'(y_0-a_1)=E[U'(Ra_1+y_1)].

Theorem: if U'''>0, a mean-preserving spread of income risk (\sigma^2\uparrow) raises saving a_1.

In one sentence. If marginal utility is convex, random income raises the average marginal utility of tomorrow's consumption, so today's consumption must fall to restore the Euler equation: saving rises.

Proof. The left side U'(y_0-a_1) rises with a_1, the right side E[U'(Ra_1+y_1)] falls, so the solution is unique. U'''>0 means U' is convex; Jensen gives E[U'(Ra_1+y_1)]>U'(Ra_1): risk shifts the right side up, so the new intersection has larger a_1. \square

Intuition. A convex marginal utility means bad luck hurts more than good luck helps, so people build a buffer. Quadratic utility (U'''=0) therefore has no precautionary saving — one of its unrealistic features. In Chapter 8, borrowing constraints plus precautionary saving have surprising aggregate implications.

Worked example (a number for precautionary saving). U=\ln c, R=\beta=1, today's income y_0=2, tomorrow's income is 1 or 3 equally likely (mean 2). Certainty equivalent: income 2 for sure gives a_1=0 (consume 2 in both periods). With risk: \dfrac1{2-a}=\dfrac12\Big(\dfrac1{1+a}+\dfrac1{3+a}\Big), i.e. (1+a)(3+a)=(2-a)(2+a), 2a^2+4a-1=0, a=\dfrac{-2+\sqrt6}2\approx0.225. The household saves about 11% of its current income purely as a buffer; with quadratic utility it would save nothing.

8. Incomplete Markets and Heterogeneity

Intuition. Complete markets insured away everyone's risk. In reality nobody can hedge their own unemployment risk. If households can self-insure only through one asset (bonds or capital) and face borrowing constraints, they must rely on precautionary saving to get through bad times. That changes aggregates: since everyone saves extra "just in case", total saving exceeds the complete-markets level and the equilibrium interest rate is below 1/\beta-1. And the wealth distribution matters: who holds how much affects aggregate demand. The three models of this chapter are cornerstones of quantitative macro.

8.1 The Huggett model

Setup: an endowment economy; a continuum of households whose income y follows a Markov chain; a single risk-free bond (price q) with borrowing constraint a'\ge-\bar A; steady state.

Household problem:

V(a,y;q)=\max\Big\{U(c)+\beta\sum_{y'}V(a',y';q)\pi(y'|y)\Big\},\quad c+qa'\le a+y,\ a'\ge-\bar A.

Recursive competitive equilibrium (steady state): a bond price q, a policy function a'=g(a,y,q) and a distribution \mu(a,y) such that ①households optimise; ②markets clear \int a\,d\mu=0 (net bond supply is zero); ③the distribution is the invariant distribution induced by the policy, \mu(a',y')=\sum_{a,y}\mathbb 1\{a'=g(a,y,q)\}\pi(y'|y)\mu(a,y).

Euler conditions:

a'=-\bar A\ \ (\text{constraint binds}),\quad\text{or}\quad qU'(c)=\beta\sum_{y'}U'(c')\pi(y'|y)\ \ (\text{interior}).

Numerical algorithm (shooting):

  1. guess q^0;
  2. for given q^j solve the household problem (value-function iteration) to get g(a,y,q^j);
  3. iterate the policy and \pi to get the invariant distribution \mu(\cdot|q^j);
  4. compute aggregate bond demand z(q^j)=\int g\,d\mu;
  5. if z>0 (demand for bonds too high) the bond is too "expensive": lower the price (q^{j+1}<q^j, higher interest rate); vice versa;
  6. iterate until |z|<\epsilon.

8.2 The Aiyagari model

Setup: like Huggett, but the saving asset is capital and there is production: a representative firm with Y=K^\alpha N^{1-\alpha}; households have heterogeneous labour endowments n (no aggregate risk) and can self-insure only by accumulating capital; steady state.

Household: V(k,n;r)=\max\{U(c)+\beta\sum_{n'}V(k',n';r)\pi(n'|n)\}, c+k'\le(r+1-\delta)k+wn, k'\ge0. Firm: the first-order conditions give r=\alpha(K/N)^{\alpha-1}-\delta and w. Equilibrium: households and the firm optimise; K=\int k\,d\mu, N=\int n\,d\mu; \mu is invariant.

Algorithm: guess r^0 → solve the household problem with w(r) → find the invariant distribution → compute aggregate capital supply K^s(r)=\int g\,d\mu and compare with the firm's capital demand K^d(r) → if there is excess supply, lower r (otherwise raise it).

Conclusion: because households over-save to self-insure, the capital supply curve goes to infinity as r\to1/\beta-1. So the equilibrium interest rate is below 1/\beta-1 (the complete-markets rate) and aggregate capital above the complete-markets level: precautionary saving causes "over-accumulation".

Why the interest rate is below 1/\beta-1. With complete markets the interest rate is pinned down by impatience: R=1/\beta, i.e. r=1/0.96-1=4.17\%. With incomplete markets and a borrowing limit every household wants a buffer (the example above shows saving of 0.225 even at R\beta=1). If R were exactly 1/\beta everyone would accumulate without limit, so the supply of capital would exceed demand; the price of saving must fall: r<4.17\% in the Aiyagari equilibrium, and the more risk, the lower r.

8.3 The Krusell–Smith model

Advanced section: the idea (approximate aggregation by one moment) is what matters.

Setup: Aiyagari plus an aggregate shock z_t (technology, Markov); households have capital as their only asset.

The difficulty: to forecast tomorrow's interest rate a household must predict tomorrow's aggregate capital, which depends on the whole wealth distribution \mu_t — an infinite-dimensional state variable.

Krusell–Smith's insight: approximate aggregation — using only the first moment of the distribution (the mean K_t) is enough to forecast, because most households' wealth hardly affects aggregates. Suppose households believe

\ln\tilde K_{t+1}=a_z+b_z\ln\tilde K_t.

Algorithm:

  1. guess (a_z^0,b_z^0);
  2. given the perceived law of motion, solve the household's recursive problem to get k'=g(k,n,z,\tilde K);
  3. simulate a long household panel and compute the aggregate capital series K_t=\frac1I\sum_ik^i_t;
  4. regress \ln K_{t+1}=a_z'+b_z'\ln K_t (by state z) for new coefficients;
  5. update and iterate until \|(a,b)^{j+1}-(a,b)^j\|<\epsilon;
  6. check that the regression R^2 is high (the approximation is good).

8.4 The overlapping-generations model (Diamond)

Intuition. In all earlier models households "live forever". In an overlapping-generations model people live only two periods: young (work and save) and old (live off savings). New people keep being born, so the economy has infinitely many households but finite-lived individuals. The competitive equilibrium need not be efficient — very different from the infinite-horizon representative-household model.

Setup: a new generation is born every period (population growth n); the young supply one unit of labour at wage W_t and save S_t; the old consume (1+r_{t+1})S_t.

\max U(C_{1,t})+\beta U(C_{2,t+1})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad C_{1,t}+S_t=W_t,\ C_{2,t+1}=(1+r_{t+1})S_t.
Firm: first-order conditions r_t=f'(k_t), W_t=f(k_t)-k_tf'(k_t). Equilibrium: capital-market clearing K_{t+1}=N_tS_t, i.e. S_t=(1+n)k_{t+1}.

Euler equation: U'(C_{1,t})=\beta(1+r_{t+1})U'(C_{2,t+1}); substituting prices gives the law of motion of capital

U'\big(f(k_t)-f'(k_t)k_t-(1+n)k_{t+1}\big)=\beta\big(1+f'(k_{t+1})\big)U'\big((1+f'(k_{t+1}))(1+n)k_{t+1}\big).
This is an implicit second-order difference equation, possibly with several steady states or even cycles.

Example (log utility + Cobb–Douglas): U=\ln c, f=k^\alpha. The young save a fraction \frac\beta{1+\beta} of wages: S_t=\frac\beta{1+\beta}W_t=\frac{\beta(1-\alpha)}{1+\beta}k_t^\alpha, so

k_{t+1}=\frac{\beta(1-\alpha)}{(1+\beta)(1+n)}\,k_t^\alpha,\qquad k^*=\Big[\frac{\beta(1-\alpha)}{(1+\beta)(1+n)}\Big]^{\frac1{1-\alpha}}.

Pareto efficiency: a planner maximises \beta U(C_{2,0})+\sum\tilde\beta^{t-1}[U(C_{1,t})+\beta U(C_{2,t+1})] s.t. C_{1,t}+\frac{C_{2,t}}{1+n}+(1+n)k_{t+1}=f(k_t)+k_t. The market equilibrium need not be Pareto efficient: if equilibrium capital is too high (f'(k)<n, dynamic inefficiency), a transfer scheme (e.g. pay-as-you-go social security) can improve every generation's welfare — an example where the First Welfare Theorem fails with infinitely many generations.

Worked example (overlapping generations). Log utility, f=k^\alpha, no population growth (n=0), full depreciation. The young save \tfrac\beta{1+\beta} of their wage W=(1-\alpha)k^\alpha. With \alpha=\tfrac13, \beta=0.6: k_{t+1}=\tfrac{0.6\cdot0.667}{1.6}k_t^{1/3}=0.25\,k_t^{1/3}, so k^*=0.25^{1.5}=0.125 and the return f'(k^*)=\tfrac13\cdot0.125^{-2/3}=1.33>1+n=1: efficient. With \alpha=0.2, \beta=1: k^*=0.4^{1.25}=0.318 and f'(k^*)=0.2\cdot0.318^{-0.8}=0.50<1: dynamically inefficient. The return on capital is below the growth rate of the economy, so a pay-as-you-go pension (take 1 from each young person, give it to each old person) gives every generation more than saving does.

9. Solving Linear Dynamic Systems

Intuition. Most macro models have no closed form. The standard recipe: (1) find the steady state; (2) log-linearise around it, turning the nonlinear system into a linear one; (3) use linear algebra to find the unique stable solution. The core is to distinguish jump variables (can adjust instantly: consumption, prices) from predetermined variables (fixed by the past: capital).

9.1 Log-linearisation

Definition. For F(x_1,\dots,x_n)=0, expand around the steady state F(\bar x)=0:

\sum_{j=1}^n\bar x_jF_j(\bar x)\,\hat x_j=0,\qquad\hat x_j=\frac{x_j-\bar x_j}{\bar x_j}.
Cheat sheet:

Level Log-linearised
f(x_t) (f(\bar x)\ne0) \dfrac{\bar xf'(\bar x)}{f(\bar x)}\hat x_t
x_ty_t \hat x_t+\hat y_t
x_t+y_t \dfrac{\bar x}{\bar x+\bar y}\hat x_t+\dfrac{\bar y}{\bar x+\bar y}\hat y_t
ax_t \hat x_t
x_t^a a\hat x_t
E_t[x_{t+1}] E_t[\hat x_{t+1}]

Worked example (checking a log-linearisation). If x_t=1.01\,\bar x and y_t=0.98\,\bar y then \hat x=0.01, \hat y=-0.02. For z=x^2/y the rule gives \hat z=2\hat x-\hat y=0.04. Exactly: 1.01^2/0.98=1.0409, a deviation of 4.1% (log 4.0%). For Y=K^\alpha N^{1-\alpha}: \hat y=\alpha\hat k+(1-\alpha)\hat n; with \alpha=\tfrac13, \hat k=3\%, \hat n=0 output rises 1%.

9.2 The Blanchard–Kahn method

Advanced section: the idea is "keep the stable solution, drop the explosive ones"; Section 9.3 shows it at work.

State-space form:

A\begin{pmatrix}E_t[y_{t+1}]\\x_{t+1}\end{pmatrix}=B\begin{pmatrix}y_t\\x_t\end{pmatrix}+G\epsilon_t,
with y_t (n-vector) the jump (forward-looking) variables and x_t (m-vector) the predetermined variables.

Conditions: A is invertible; A^{-1}B diagonalises as V^{-1}\Lambda V; let k be the number of eigenvalues with modulus above 1.

Theorem (Blanchard–Kahn):

  • k=n (number of unstable roots equals number of jump variables) ⟹ a unique stable solution;
  • k<n ⟹ multiple solutions (indeterminacy, sunspots);
  • k>n ⟹ no solution (all paths explode).

In one sentence. Rotate the system so that each unstable direction becomes its own equation; an unstable equation can only stay bounded if its variable equals the discounted sum of future shocks, which pins down the jump variables.

Procedure. Order \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(D_{nn},D_{mm}) with |\lambda|>1 first, and partition V and VA^{-1}G=(C_n;C_m) likewise. The first block of equations is

V_{nn}E_t[y_{t+1}]+V_{nm}x_{t+1}=D_{nn}(V_{nn}y_t+V_{nm}x_t)+C_n\epsilon_t.
Let T_t=V_{nn}y_t+V_{nm}x_t, so E_tT_{t+1}=D_{nn}T_t+C_n\epsilon_t. Since every diagonal entry of D_{nn} exceeds 1, solve forward to infinity:
T_t=-D_{nn}^{-1}\sum_{i\ge0}\big(D_{nn}^{i}\big)^{-1}C_nE_t[\epsilon_{t+i}]
(the terminal term (D_{nn}^N)^{-1}E_tT_{t+N}\to0 is precisely the transversality condition). This gives the policy function
y_t=-V_{nn}^{-1}V_{nm}x_t-V_{nn}^{-1}\sum_{i\ge0}(D_{nn}^i)^{-1}D_{nn}^{-1}C_nE_t[\epsilon_{t+i}].

9.3 Example: the stochastic neoclassical growth model

Planner: \max E_0\sum\beta^t\ln c_t, c_t+k_{t+1}-(1-\delta)k_t=a_tk_t^\alpha, \ln a_{t+1}=\rho\ln a_t+e_{t+1}.

First-order condition: \dfrac1{c_t}=\beta E_t\Big[\dfrac1{c_{t+1}}(\alpha a_{t+1}k_{t+1}^{\alpha-1}+1-\delta)\Big]. Steady state: \alpha\bar k^{\alpha-1}=\dfrac1\beta-1+\delta, \bar c=\bar k^\alpha-\delta\bar k. After log-linearisation: a state-space form (c jump, k predetermined, a_t an exogenous state) from which Blanchard–Kahn gives the linear policy \hat c_t=\eta_{ck}\hat k_t+\eta_{ca}a_t.

Worked example (the Ramsey model linearised). Log utility, f=k^{1/3}, \beta=0.96, \delta=0.1, so \bar k=3.61, \bar c=1.17. The Euler equation and the resource constraint, linearised in log deviations, give

\begin{pmatrix}\hat c_{t+1}\\\hat k_{t+1}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1.029&-0.094\\-0.325&1.042\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\hat c_t\\\hat k_t\end{pmatrix},
with eigenvalues 0.860 and 1.211. One root is below 1 and one above: a saddle; there is one jump variable (c) and one unstable root, so Blanchard–Kahn holds and the solution is unique. The stable eigenvector gives the policy \hat c_t=0.558\,\hat k_t and \hat k_{t+1}=0.860\,\hat k_t. If capital starts 10% above its steady state, consumption starts 5.6% above its steady state and 14% of the gap closes each period (half-life \ln0.5/\ln0.86\approx4.6 periods).

10. Real Business Cycles

Intuition. The striking claim of real-business-cycle (RBC) theory: no monetary shocks and no price stickiness are needed — random technology shocks alone, through households' intertemporal choices (consumption smoothing, labour–leisure substitution) and capital accumulation, can generate aggregate fluctuations resembling the data. This is a world of perfect competition, complete markets and optimality: the cycle is an optimal response to shocks, not a "failure".

10.1 The planner's RBC model

Setup: separable utility U(c,n)=\ln c+\theta\ln(1-n); technology Y=Ak^\alpha(Xn)^{1-\alpha} with X growing at rate \gamma; endogenous labour supply; capital accumulation.

\max E_0\sum\beta^t\big[\ln c_t+\theta\ln(1-N_t)\big]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad c_t+\gamma k_{t+1}=a_tk_t^\alpha N_t^{1-\alpha}+(1-\delta)k_t,\quad\ln a_t=\rho\ln a_{t-1}+e_t.
(Variables are detrended by X_t.)

First-order conditions (\lambda_t=1/c_t):

\begin{aligned}\lambda_t(1-\alpha)a_tk_t^\alpha N_t^{-\alpha}&=\frac\theta{1-N_t}\quad(\text{labour–leisure: }MRS=\text{wage}),\\\lambda_t\gamma&=\beta E_t\big[\lambda_{t+1}(\alpha a_{t+1}k_{t+1}^{\alpha-1}N_{t+1}^{1-\alpha}+1-\delta)\big]\quad(\text{Euler}).\end{aligned}

Steady state: \dfrac\gamma\beta-1+\delta=\alpha(k/N)^{\alpha-1}, so the capital–labour ratio is \dfrac kN=\Big[\dfrac\alpha{\gamma/\beta-1+\delta}\Big]^{\frac1{1-\alpha}} and the other steady-state variables follow. Then log-linearise and solve by Blanchard–Kahn.

Mechanism: a positive technology shock raises wages and the return to capital ⟹ households engage in intertemporal substitution: work more and invest more now, because work pays more now ⟹ output, investment and employment rise together; a persistent shock (large \rho) lets capital accumulation stretch the effect out.

Worked example (the steady state of an RBC economy). Quarterly data: \alpha=\tfrac13, \beta=0.99, \delta=0.025. The capital–output ratio is \bar k/\bar y=\alpha/(1/\beta-1+\delta)=0.333/0.0351=9.5 quarters (2.4 years of output). Investment is \delta\bar k/\bar y=0.2375 of output, so consumption is 76% of output: realistic shares come out of three parameters. A shock to \ln a_t with persistence \rho=0.95 fades only slowly, so the investment boom it triggers is stretched over many quarters.

10.2 Decentralisation

Advanced section.

Households own capital: households choose consumption and investment I_t=\gamma k_{t+1}-(1-\delta)k_t, with budget c_t+I_t=w_tN_t+R_tk_t+\pi_t; firms rent capital and labour, maximising a_tk_t^\alpha N_t^{1-\alpha}-w_tN_t-R_tk_t. Markets clear: c_t+I_t=Y_t.

Tobin's q: let \lambda_t,\mu_t be the shadow prices of consumption and investment; q_t=\mu_t/\lambda_t is the value of an additional unit of capital relative to its cost. The household wants to invest when q_t>1.

Firms own capital: households trade firm shares S_t; the firm discounts profits at shareholders' SDF, \max E_t[m_{t,t+1}\pi_t] with \pi_t=Y_t-w_tN_t-I_t.

Conclusion: with homogeneous (constant-returns) technology both decentralisations deliver an equilibrium that coincides with the planner's solution (welfare theorems). So we may study the RBC economy by solving the planner's problem.

11. Money and the Classical Dichotomy

Intuition. What is money? Why would people hold non-interest-bearing paper? The simplest answer: paper money itself gives utility (convenience, liquidity) — "money in the utility function". The classical dichotomy says: in an economy with perfectly flexible prices, real variables (output, employment, the real wage, the real interest rate) are determined entirely by technology and preferences, while nominal variables (the price level, nominal interest rate, money supply) merely fix "the unit of account". Monetary policy can only determine nominal variables.

11.1 The dichotomy model

Setup: households \max E_0\sum\beta^tU(C_t,N_t), budget P_tC_t+Q_tB_t=B_{t-1}+W_tN_t+\Pi_t (bond price Q_t, nominal rate i_t=1/Q_t); firms \max P_tY_t-W_tN_t, Y_t=A_tN_t^{1-\alpha}; clearing Y_t=C_t, B_t=0.

First-order conditions: \lambda_tP_t=U_C, \lambda_tW_t=-U_N, \lambda_tQ_t=\beta E_t[\lambda_{t+1}]; firm (1-\alpha)P_tA_tN_t^{-\alpha}=W_t.

Log-linearised (with U=\dfrac{C^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}-\dfrac{N^{1+\phi}}{1+\phi}), the real variables are determined independently by five equations:

\hat w_t-\hat p_t=\phi\hat n_t+\sigma\hat c_t,\quad\hat w_t-\hat p_t=a_t-\alpha\hat n_t,\quad\hat y_t=a_t+(1-\alpha)\hat n_t,\quad\hat y_t=\hat c_t,\quad\hat b_t=0.
Solving,
\hat y_t=\frac{1+\phi}{\alpha+\phi+\sigma(1-\alpha)}\,a_t.
This does not involve any nominal variable — this is the classical dichotomy.

But nominal variables are not pinned down: there is one more unknown than equations, so we need a monetary policy rule.

Worked example (what a technology shock does when money is neutral). \sigma=1, \phi=1, \alpha=\tfrac13: \hat y_t=\dfrac{1+\phi}{\alpha+\phi+\sigma(1-\alpha)}a_t=\dfrac{2}{0.333+1+0.667}a_t=a_t. A 1% technology shock raises output by 1%, whatever the central bank does; the central bank affects only the price level and the nominal interest rate.

11.2 Policy rules and the price level

Fisher equation: from the Euler equation \hat i_t=\hat r_t+E_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}], where \hat r_t=\sigma E_t[\hat y_{t+1}-\hat y_t] is the real interest rate (determined by real variables).

  • Exogenous interest-rate rule: \hat i_t is an exogenous stationary process. Then E_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}]=\hat i_t-\hat r_t fixes only expected inflation, not the actual price level — indeterminacy (sunspot equilibria).
  • Endogenous feedback rule: \hat i_t=\phi_\pi\hat\pi_t+\epsilon_t. Substituting into the Fisher equation,
    \hat\pi_t=\frac1{\phi_\pi}E_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}]+\frac1{\phi_\pi}(\hat r_t-\epsilon_t).
    Taylor principle: if \phi_\pi>1, by Blanchard–Kahn (inflation is a jump variable and there is exactly one unstable root) the price path is unique; if \phi_\pi\le1 it is indeterminate.

Intuition: if inflation rises by 1% and the central bank raises the nominal rate by more than 1% (the real rate rises), demand is dampened and inflation falls back — anchoring the price path. If the bank responds too little, any self-fulfilling inflation expectation can be an equilibrium.

Worked example (the Taylor principle in one line). Take \hat\pi_t=\tfrac1{\phi_\pi}E_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}]+\tfrac1{\phi_\pi}u_t with u_t=\hat r_t-\epsilon_t. With \phi_\pi=1.5 and a shock that lasts one period (u_0=1) inflation today is \hat\pi_0=\tfrac1{1.5}\cdot1=0.667 and zero afterwards: a unique path. With \phi_\pi=0.8 the coefficient 1/\phi_\pi=1.25 is above one: solving forward diverges, so many (even self-fulfilling) paths are consistent with the equation.

11.3 Money in the utility function

Setup: utility U(C_t,N_t,M_t/P_t), budget P_tC_t+Q_tB_t+M_t=B_{t-1}+W_tN_t+M_{t-1}+\Pi_t+P_tT_t; the government returns seigniorage through transfers T_t=(M_t-M_{t-1})/P_t.

First-order condition for money: \beta E_t[\lambda_{t+1}]-\lambda_t+\dfrac1{P_t}U_M=0. Combined with the bond condition \lambda_tQ_t=\beta E_t\lambda_{t+1},

U_M=\lambda_tP_t(1-Q_t)=U_C\cdot\frac{i_t}{1+i_t}.

Reading: 1-Q_t=\dfrac{i_t}{1+i_t} is the implicit price of holding cash (forgone bond interest). Money, like consumption and leisure, has marginal utility proportional to its price.

With U=\dfrac{C^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}-\dfrac{N^{1+\phi}}{1+\phi}+\dfrac{(M/P)^{1-v}}{1-v}, log-linearisation gives the money demand function

\hat m_t-\hat p_t=\frac\sigma v\hat y_t-\frac1{v(1-\beta)}\hat i_t.
The real-variable equations are unchanged — money remains neutral (the "dichotomy" still holds); money demand simply determines the quantity of money after the fact.

11.4 Optimal monetary policy: the Friedman rule

Assume local satiation in money: there is \bar M with U_M=0. A planner with no monetary friction maximises U(C,M/P,N) s.t. C=AN^{1-\alpha}, giving U_M=0. Comparing with the household's condition U_M=U_C\dfrac{i}{1+i} requires

\boxed{\ i^*=0\ }.
Friedman rule: the optimal nominal interest rate is zero. By the Fisher equation E_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}]=-\hat r_t<0: optimal inflation is negative (minus the real rate) — deflation makes cash pay as much as bonds, so holding cash is not "taxed".

Worked example (the Friedman rule). With \beta=0.96 the real rate is 1/0.96-1=4.17\%. The Friedman rule sets i=0 so, by the Fisher equation, optimal inflation is -4.17\% a year: prices fall by about 4% a year so that cash, which pays no interest, earns the same real return as bonds.

12. The New Keynesian Model

Intuition. In the classical-dichotomy world monetary policy changes only nominal variables. The data say it has real effects. The New Keynesian model has two core assumptions: (1) firms are monopolistically competitive — they have pricing power, so price is their choice; (2) prices are sticky — only a fraction of firms can change prices each period. So when the central bank changes the nominal rate, prices cannot adjust immediately, the real interest rate and real demand move, and monetary policy has real effects.

12.1 Monopolistic competition and Dixit–Stiglitz

Setup: a continuum j\in[0,1] of firms, each producing a differentiated good with Y_{jt}=Z_tN_{jt} and each a monopolist in its own product; prices temporarily flexible.

Dixit–Stiglitz aggregator: C_t=\Big[\int_0^1C_{jt}^{\frac{\theta-1}\theta}dj\Big]^{\frac\theta{\theta-1}}, with \theta>1 the elasticity of substitution.

Consumer cost minimisation: \min\int P_{jt}C_{jt}dj s.t. C_t\ge a given level. The first-order condition gives the demand for good j

C_{jt}=\Big(\frac{P_{jt}}{P_t}\Big)^{-\theta}C_t,\qquad P_t=\Big[\int_0^1P_{jt}^{1-\theta}dj\Big]^{\frac1{1-\theta}},
and P_tC_t=\int P_{jt}C_{jt}dj. (The price elasticity of demand is \theta.)

Household: \max E_0\sum\beta^t\Big[\dfrac{C_t^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}-\chi\dfrac{N_t^{1+\eta}}{1+\eta}\Big]. Linearised first-order conditions:

\hat w_t-\hat p_t=\eta\hat n_t+\sigma\hat c_t,\qquad\hat c_t=E_t[\hat c_{t+1}]-\frac1\sigma\big(\hat i_t-E_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}]\big).

Firm: facing demand (P_{jt}/P_t)^{-\theta}Y_t, maximise unit profit times quantity: \Big[\dfrac{P_{jt}}{P_t}-\varphi_t\Big]\Big(\dfrac{P_{jt}}{P_t}\Big)^{-\theta}Y_t, where \varphi_t=\dfrac{W_t}{P_tZ_t} is the real marginal cost. First-order condition:

\frac{P_{jt}}{P_t}=\frac\theta{\theta-1}\varphi_t\quad(\text{price = markup × marginal cost}).
In the symmetric equilibrium P_{jt}=P_t and, after linearisation, \hat\varphi_t=0, i.e. \hat w_t-\hat p_t=\hat z_t (ignoring the constant markup).

Flexible-price equilibrium: combining \hat w-\hat p=\hat z, \hat w-\hat p=\eta\hat n+\sigma\hat c, \hat y=\hat c=\hat z+\hat n:

\hat y_t^f=\frac{1+\eta}{\eta+\sigma}\hat z_t\quad(\text{natural output}),
with real rate \hat r^f_t=\sigma E_t[\hat y^f_{t+1}-\hat y^f_t] (the natural rate).

Worked example (the markup and natural output). With \theta=6 the markup is \tfrac\theta{\theta-1}=1.2: each firm charges 20% above marginal cost (which also makes the natural level of output lower than the efficient level). With \eta=\sigma=1, natural output is \hat y^f_t=\dfrac{1+\eta}{\eta+\sigma}\hat z_t=\hat z_t: a 1% technology shock raises natural output 1%.

12.2 Calvo sticky prices

Setup: each period only a fraction 1-\omega of firms (randomly drawn) can reset prices; the rest keep their old price; \omega is the probability a price stays fixed (average price duration 1/(1-\omega)).

A resetting firm chooses P_{jt} to maximise expected discounted profit while the price remains in force:

\max\sum_{i=0}^\infty(\omega\beta)^im_{t,t+i}\Big[\frac{P_{jt}}{P_{t+i}}-\varphi_{t+i}\Big]\Big(\frac{P_{jt}}{P_{t+i}}\Big)^{-\theta}C_{t+i}.
Linearised first-order condition:
\hat p_{jt}=(1-\omega\beta)\sum_{i=0}^\infty(\omega\beta)^i\big(\hat p_{t+i}+\hat\varphi_{t+i}\big).

Intuition: the optimal reset price is a weighted average of all future marginal costs (plus the price level), with weights falling as "probability the price is still in force × discounting". Since the price may stay stuck for many periods the firm must look ahead at future costs.

Price index: P_t^{1-\theta}=(1-\omega)P_{jt}^{1-\theta}+\omega P_{t-1}^{1-\theta}; linearised \hat p_t=(1-\omega)\hat p_{jt}+\omega\hat p_{t-1}, i.e. \hat\pi_t=(1-\omega)(\hat p_{jt}-\hat p_{t-1}).

The New Keynesian Phillips curve (NKPC). Writing the reset-price formula in difference form and substituting the price index,

\boxed{\ \hat\pi_t=\beta E_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}]+\kappa\,\hat\varphi_t,\qquad\kappa=\frac{(1-\omega)(1-\omega\beta)}\omega\ }.
With \hat\varphi_t=(\eta+\sigma)(\hat y_t-\hat y_t^f)\equiv(\eta+\sigma)\hat x_t (the output gap x_t),
\hat\pi_t=\beta E_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}]+\tilde\kappa\,\hat x_t,\qquad\tilde\kappa=\frac{(1-\omega)(1-\omega\beta)(\eta+\sigma)}\omega.
(Below, for brevity, the slope is again written \kappa: \pi_t=\beta E_t\pi_{t+1}+\kappa x_t.)

Reading: inflation = discounted expected future inflation + pressure from the output gap. The stickier prices (larger \omega), the smaller \kappa, and the less inflation responds to the gap.

Dynamic IS curve: subtract the flexible-price Euler equation from the sticky one:

\hat x_t=E_t[\hat x_{t+1}]-\frac1\sigma\big(\hat i_t-E_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}]-\hat r_t^f\big).

Intuition: if the real rate i-E\pi exceeds the natural rate, people postpone consumption and the gap is negative.

Worked example (the slope of the Phillips curve). \omega=0.75 (a price is fixed for 4 quarters on average), \beta=0.99, \sigma=\eta=1: \kappa=\dfrac{(1-\omega)(1-\omega\beta)}{\omega}=\dfrac{0.25\cdot0.2575}{0.75}=0.0858 and the slope on the output gap is \tilde\kappa=\kappa(\eta+\sigma)=0.172. If the gap is +1\% and expected inflation is 0, quarterly inflation is 0.17\% (about 0.7% a year). With less stickiness, \omega=0.5, \kappa=0.505 and \tilde\kappa=1.01: six times steeper. Stickier prices flatten the Phillips curve: it takes a bigger gap to move inflation. The weights in the figure show why: a firm that may keep its price for years puts weight on distant costs.

12.3 The three-equation model and the Taylor rule

Three equations: the NKPC, the dynamic IS and a policy rule, for instance the Taylor rule

\hat i_t=\phi_\pi\hat\pi_t+\phi_x\hat x_t+e_t.
Determinacy (Blanchard–Kahn): inflation and the gap are both jump variables, so two unstable roots are needed.

  • i_t=e_t (exogenous rate) ⟹ indeterminate;
  • i_t=\phi_\pi\pi_t+e_t with \phi_\pi>1 ⟹ determinate;
  • i_t=\phi_\pi\pi_t+\phi_xx_t+e_t: \phi_\pi+\dfrac{1-\beta}\kappa\phi_x>1 ⟹ determinate (the general Taylor principle).

Worked example (checking determinacy). With \tilde\kappa=0.172, \beta=0.99: (1-\beta)/\tilde\kappa=0.058. Take \phi_\pi=1.5, \phi_x=0.5: 1.5+0.058\cdot0.5=1.53>1 determinate. Take \phi_\pi=0.9, \phi_x=1.5: 0.9+0.058\cdot1.5=0.987<1 indeterminate: a central bank that responds weakly to inflation (even if it reacts to the gap) cannot rule out self-fulfilling inflation.

13. Optimal Monetary Policy

Intuition. How should the central bank set rates? The NK model has two distortions: (1) price stickiness ties inflation to the output gap; (2) sometimes there are cost-push shocks (an oil price rise): they raise inflation and lower output at once, and the bank must trade off. We first see the happy case without cost-push shocks, then the trade-off with them, and finally compare worlds where the bank can and cannot commit to future policy.

13.1 No cost-push shock: the divine coincidence

Theorem (divine coincidence). Without cost-push shocks, optimal monetary policy sets the interest rate to follow the natural rate, i_t=r_t^f+\phi_\pi\pi_t (\phi_\pi>1), which simultaneously delivers zero inflation and a zero output gap.

In one sentence. Inflation is the discounted sum of future output gaps, so a zero gap for ever means zero inflation for ever, and the interest rate that delivers a zero gap is the natural rate.

Proof. Solving the NKPC forward, \pi_t=\kappa\sum_{i\ge0}\beta^iE_t[x_{t+i}]. If x_t\equiv0 then \pi_t\equiv0. The dynamic IS shows x\equiv0 is a solution when i_t=r_t^f, and \phi_\pi>1 rules out other solutions. \square

The rate i_t=r_t^f is the Wicksellian rate (natural rate).

The "coincidence": stabilising inflation and stabilising the gap do not conflict: by stabilising inflation the bank automatically stabilises the gap.

13.2 Cost-push shocks: the inflation–output trade-off

Central bank's loss function:

\min\ \frac12E_t\sum_{i=0}^\infty\beta^i\big(\pi_{t+i}^2+\lambda x_{t+i}^2\big)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\pi_t=\beta E_t\pi_{t+1}+\kappa x_t+e_t,
where e_t is the cost-push shock. (The loss can be derived as a second-order approximation to household welfare; \lambda is the relative weight on the gap.)

Discretion (no commitment). The bank re-optimises every period, taking E_t\pi_{t+1} as given. The first-order conditions \pi_t+\psi_t=0, \lambda x_t-\kappa\psi_t=0 give the targeting rule

\pi_t=-\frac\lambda\kappa x_t\quad(\text{lean against the wind: high inflation, push the gap down}).
For i.i.d. shocks, combining with the NKPC:
x_t=-\frac\kappa{\lambda+\kappa^2}e_t,\qquad\pi_t=\frac\lambda{\lambda+\kappa^2}e_t.
Implementing interest-rate rule: i_t=r_t^f+\sigma(E_tx_{t+1}-x_t)+E_t\pi_{t+1}=r_t^f+\dfrac{\sigma\kappa}{\lambda+\kappa^2}e_t, plus a term \phi_\pi(\pi_t-\pi_t^*) (\phi_\pi>1) to ensure determinacy.

Commitment. The bank can commit at t=0 to the whole path. First-order conditions (with \psi_{-1}=0):

\pi_{t}+\psi_t-\psi_{t-1}=0,\qquad\lambda x_t-\kappa\psi_t=0.
Eliminating \psi gives the targeting rule from a timeless perspective
\pi_t=-\frac\lambda\kappa\big(x_t-x_{t-1}\big).

Key difference: under commitment the bank cares about changes in the gap, so after a shock it keeps the gap negative for a while (pulling down future inflation expectations), so current inflation rises less — the response to the impact is smaller but more persistent. This policy is time-inconsistent: once the shock has passed, the bank would like to "re-optimise", breaking its earlier promise.

Why is commitment better? In the NKPC today's inflation depends on expected future inflation. Commitment lets the bank "borrow" the future to improve today's trade-off — leverage that discretion cannot obtain.

Worked example (discretion vs commitment). \kappa=0.2, \lambda=0.1, \beta=0.99; a one-off cost-push shock e_0=1.

impact x_0 impact \pi_0 after impact loss
Discretion -\kappa/(\lambda+\kappa^2)=-1.43 \lambda/(\lambda+\kappa^2)=0.71 back to 0 at once 0.357
Commitment -1.08 0.54 x: -0.58,-0.31,-0.17,\dots; \pi negative: -0.25,-0.13,\dots 0.269

Check discretion: \pi=\kappa x+e=0.2\cdot(-1.43)+1=0.71 ✓. Under commitment the central bank promises to keep the gap negative for a while and to tolerate below-target inflation afterwards; because firms believe this, inflation today rises less (0.54 against 0.71) and output falls less (1.08 against 1.43). The price of this is a promise the bank will be tempted to break once the shock is over: time inconsistency.

13.3 Extension: inflation inertia

Advanced section.

Add inflation inertia (some firms index to past inflation): the NKPC becomes

\pi_t=\beta(1-\phi)E_t\pi_{t+1}+\phi\pi_{t-1}+\kappa x_t+e_t.

  • Commitment: first-order conditions \pi_t-\psi_t+(1-\phi)\psi_{t-1}+\phi\beta E_t\psi_{t+1}=0, \lambda x_t+\kappa\psi_t=0 (\psi_{-1}=0); time inconsistency persists.
  • Discretion: inflation is a state variable, with value function V(\pi_{t-1},e_t); guess linear policies \pi_t=A_1\pi_{t-1}+A_2e_t, x_t=B_1\pi_{t-1}+B_2e_t and solve for the coefficients by guess-and-verify (introducing the multiplier guess \theta_t=C_1\pi_{t-1}+C_2e_t).

14. Looking Back: One Thread

The many macro models are the same skeleton with a little added or removed:

Model Preferences Technology Market structure Key result

Ramsey optimal saving same planner Euler equation, saddle-path stability

Arrow–Debreu CRRA etc. endowment complete markets risk sharing; welfare theorems; SDF pricing

Ideas to take away:

  • The Euler equation is the "Newton's law" of dynamic macro: at the margin, the loss from giving up a unit of consumption today equals tomorrow's gain; with the transversality condition it rules out impossible paths.
  • Recursion turns an infinite-dimensional problem into a functional equation; the contraction mapping guarantees existence, uniqueness and computability.
  • Complete markets ⟹ risk sharing ⟹ a representative household; incomplete markets ⟹ precautionary saving ⟹ distributions matter.
  • The SDF unifies asset pricing: risk premia are covariances with the SDF.
  • Saddle-path stability / Blanchard–Kahn: as many unstable roots as jump variables ⟺ unique equilibrium; this is also the mathematical core of the Taylor principle.
  • Nominal stickiness + forward-looking pricing give monetary policy real effects; expectations (commitment) make policy more powerful.
