15. Common Misconceptions

Misconception Correct
The Solow saving rate is chosen optimally It is exogenous; only the Ramsey model chooses saving, and its steady state has less capital than the golden rule
Poor countries always catch up Only conditional convergence: if they share the same saving rate, technology and population growth
A larger discount factor \beta means more impatience \beta close to 1 means more patient (the future is discounted less)
The Bellman equation is just a trick It encodes the principle of optimality; the contraction property guarantees a unique solution and convergent iteration
Higher unemployment benefits raise unemployment only by "laziness" They raise the reservation wage and the bargained wage, which lowers vacancy creation
Complete markets mean everyone is equal Everyone's consumption is a fixed share of the aggregate; shares depend on the present value of endowments
The equity premium puzzle says stocks are mispriced It says the simple C-CAPM needs implausibly high risk aversion; richer models (habits, long-run risk) address it
Permanent-income theory says consumption never reacts to income It reacts to revisions of expected permanent income; transitory changes are mostly saved
Precautionary saving needs risk aversion only It needs prudence (U'''>0); quadratic utility is risk averse but not prudent
Incomplete markets leave the interest rate unchanged The interest rate falls below 1/\beta-1 because of self-insurance
Log-linearised models are exact They are first-order approximations around the steady state; they miss large shocks and risk premia
Blanchard–Kahn finds a solution It counts roots: unique solution only if unstable roots = jump variables
RBC says recessions are bad RBC says recessions are an optimal response to productivity shocks; policy cannot help
Money neutrality means monetary policy does nothing In the flexible-price model it moves only nominal variables; with sticky prices it moves real ones too
The Taylor principle means "raise rates a lot" It means raise the nominal rate by more than one-for-one with inflation, so the real rate rises
Commitment is just better rules It uses the effect of expected future policy on today's inflation, but it is time-inconsistent

16. Exercises with Answers

1. Solow with f(k)=\sqrt k, g=0, \delta=0.1, s=0.2. Find k^*,y^*,c^*, the golden-rule saving rate and say whether the economy under- or over-saves.

Answer. 0.1k=0.2\sqrt k\Rightarrow\sqrt k=2, k^*=4, y^*=2, c^*=0.8\cdot2=1.6. Golden rule: s=\alpha=0.5, k=(0.5/0.1)^2=25, c=5-2.5=2.5>1.6. The economy under-saves.

2. Ramsey with f=\sqrt k, \delta=0.1, \beta=0.9. Find the steady state.

Answer. f'(\bar k)=1/0.9-1+0.1=0.2111, so 0.5\bar k^{-1/2}=0.2111, \bar k=5.61, \bar c=\sqrt{5.61}-0.561=1.81 (compare the Solow golden rule 25, which would need \beta=1: impatience lowers capital).

3. Brock–Mirman with \alpha=0.3, \beta=0.9. Find the saving rate, k_1,c_0 from k_0=1, the coefficient A and the steady state.

Answer. \alpha\beta=0.27, so k_1=0.27, c_0=0.73; A=0.3/0.73=0.411; \bar k=0.27^{1/0.7}=0.154.

4. P=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.2\\0.4&0.6\end{pmatrix}. Find the stationary distribution and the expected duration of state 1.

Answer. \psi_1=0.8\psi_1+0.4\psi_2\Rightarrow\psi_1=2\psi_2, so \psi=(2/3,1/3). Duration of state 1: 1/0.2=5 periods.

5. McCall: offers uniform on [0,1], b=0.2, \beta=0.9. Find the reservation wage, the acceptance probability and the expected duration.

Answer. \bar w=0.2+4.5(1-\bar w)^2. With u=1-\bar w: 4.5u^2+u-0.8=0, u=0.325, so \bar w=0.675; acceptance 0.325; duration 3.08 periods.

6. Complete markets, one period, two equally likely states, log utility, aggregate endowment (3,1). Agent 1 has (3,0) and agent 2 has (0,1). Find the consumption of each.

Answer. State prices p_H=\tfrac16, p_L=\tfrac12. PV of agent 1: 3\cdot\tfrac16=0.5; of agent 2: 1\cdot\tfrac12=0.5. Each has share \tfrac12: c^1=c^2=(1.5,0.5).

7. Lucas tree, log utility, \beta=0.9. Find P/d, and with d=2, next dividend 1.8 or 2.2 equally likely, the bond price and the risk-free rate.

Answer. P/d=\beta/(1-\beta)=9, so P=18. Q=0.9\cdot\tfrac12(2/1.8+2/2.2)=0.9\cdot1.0101=0.909, R^f=1/Q=1.10.

8. PIH with r=4\% and zero assets. By how much does consumption rise if income rises by 100 (a) for one period, (b) with persistence \rho=0.5, (c) permanently?

Answer. (a) \tfrac{0.04}{1.04}\cdot100=3.85; (b) \tfrac{0.04}{1.04-0.5}\cdot100=7.41; (c) 100.

9. Two periods, U=\ln c, R=\beta=1, y_0=2, y_1\in\{1,3\} equally likely. Find saving.

Answer. \tfrac1{2-a}=\tfrac12(\tfrac1{1+a}+\tfrac1{3+a}) gives 2a^2+4a-1=0, a=(\sqrt6-2)/2=0.225.

10. OLG with log utility, \alpha=0.3, \beta=0.8, n=0. Find k^* and say whether the steady state is dynamically efficient.

Answer. k_{t+1}=\tfrac{0.8\cdot0.7}{1.8}k_t^{0.3}=0.311k_t^{0.3}, k^*=0.311^{1/0.7}=0.189; f'(k^*)=0.3\cdot0.189^{-0.7}=0.964<1+n=1: slightly dynamically inefficient.

11. z=x^2/y with x=1.01\bar x, y=0.98\bar y. Compute \hat z by the log-linear rule and exactly.

Answer. Rule: 2(0.01)-(-0.02)=0.04. Exactly 1.01^2/0.98=1.0409 (4.1%; log 4.0%).

12. A model has one jump variable. Decide uniqueness if the eigenvalues are (a) 0.8,1.3; (b) 0.8,0.9; (c) 1.2,1.3.

Answer. (a) one unstable root = one jump variable: unique; (b) no unstable root: indeterminate; (c) two unstable roots: no solution.

13. NK with \beta=0.99, \sigma=\eta=1. Find \tilde\kappa for \omega=0.5 and \omega=0.75 and check determinacy of \phi_\pi=0.9, \phi_x=1.5 for \omega=0.75.

Answer. \omega=0.5: \kappa=0.505, \tilde\kappa=1.01. \omega=0.75: \kappa=0.0858, \tilde\kappa=0.172. Determinacy: 0.9+\tfrac{0.01}{0.172}\cdot1.5=0.987<1: indeterminate.

14. Discretion with \kappa=0.2, \lambda=0.2 and a unit cost-push shock. Find x_0 and \pi_0 and say what happens as \lambda\to\infty.

Answer. \kappa^2=0.04: x_0=-0.2/0.24=-0.833, \pi_0=0.2/0.24=0.833. As \lambda\to\infty, x_0\to0 and \pi_0\to1: a central bank that only cares about the gap lets the cost-push shock pass through fully into inflation.

17. Glossary

Term Meaning
Steady state a state in which all (detrended) variables stop changing
Golden rule the saving rate (capital) that maximises steady-state consumption
Conditional convergence poorer countries grow faster given the same fundamentals
Euler equation at the optimum, the utility cost of saving one more unit equals the discounted gain
Transversality condition capital cannot be hoarded for ever unused
Saddle path the unique path that leads to the steady state
Bellman equation V(x)=\max\{F+\beta V(x')\}: the recursive form of an optimisation problem
Contraction mapping an operator that shrinks distances, so iteration converges to a unique fixed point
Policy function the optimal choice as a function of the state
Markov chain random states whose next-period distribution depends only on today's state
Stationary distribution the distribution that is unchanged by the chain's transition
Reservation wage the lowest wage an unemployed worker accepts
Matching function the number of new matches as a function of unemployed and vacancies
Tightness \theta vacancies per unemployed worker
Beveridge curve the negative relation between unemployment and vacancies
Nash bargaining splitting the surplus of a match according to bargaining power
Complete markets a contingent claim for every state of the world
Arrow security a claim that pays 1 in one state only
Stochastic discount factor (SDF) the intertemporal marginal rate of substitution that prices payoffs
Risk premium the expected excess return that compensates for covariance with the SDF
Equity premium puzzle the premium is much larger than C-CAPM with sensible risk aversion implies
Permanent-income hypothesis consumption follows the annuity value of lifetime resources
Prudence U'''>0; the motive to save more when risk rises
Incomplete markets not every risk can be insured; households self-insure with assets
Borrowing constraint a limit on how negative assets may be
Overlapping generations a model in which finite-lived people of different ages coexist
Dynamic inefficiency the return on capital is below the economy's growth rate
Log-linearisation expressing a model in percentage deviations from its steady state, to first order
Jump / predetermined variable one that can change immediately / one fixed by the past
Blanchard–Kahn condition unstable roots equal jump variables, so the solution is unique
Tobin's q the value of an additional unit of capital relative to its cost
Classical dichotomy real variables are determined without reference to money
Fisher equation nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation
Friedman rule the optimal nominal interest rate is zero
Monopolistic competition many firms, each a price-setter for its own variety
Calvo pricing each period a random fraction of firms may reset its price
New Keynesian Phillips curve \pi_t=\beta E_t\pi_{t+1}+\kappa x_t
Output gap output minus the flexible-price (natural) output
Natural rate the real rate that would prevail with flexible prices
Taylor rule / Taylor principle a rule i=\phi_\pi\pi+\phi_xx; determinacy needs the real rate to rise with inflation
Divine coincidence with no cost-push shocks, stabilising inflation also stabilises the gap
Cost-push shock a shock that raises inflation and lowers output at once
Discretion / commitment re-optimising every period / binding oneself to a whole future path
Time inconsistency the promised path is no longer optimal when the time comes
